messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Navy Officer
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Crowding: Crowded places, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Avoid Friends: avoid seeing friends, Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 34, Nathan had been a Navy officer long enough to think of himself as steady under pressure, someone other people looked to when things turned chaotic. The disaster that undid that certainty came during a coastal deployment when a severe storm surge struck with little warning and drove water through the lower levels of the building where he and others had taken shelter. He remembers the crush of bodies trying to force through a narrow passage, the lights failing, and the air turning sour with spilled liquor from a ruptured storage area mixed with seawater and fuel. In his memory the event comes less as a story than as stark, disconnected images: shoulders pressed against him, black water rising, a doorway he could not reach. When it hits him, his body stiffens into the same braced, pinned position he had been in then, as if he is still wedged in place waiting for another wave. At times the memory feels so unreal that he catches himself thinking it cannot have happened to him at all, and that unreality is part of what unsettles him.

In the months afterward, Nathan found that certain moments in ordinary life on base or off duty seemed to seize him before he understood why. A crowded corridor aboard ship, a packed commissary aisle, stepping into a dim room, or returning to physical locations along the waterfront could bring back vivid visual flashes of that night. The smell of alcohol was especially potent; if he passed a bar near the harbor or caught liquor on someone’s breath, he was abruptly back in those images, his muscles locking and his body remembering the posture of entrapment. He began organizing his days around not letting that happen. He waited for empty elevators, avoided social gatherings with friends, and made excuses to leave any place that felt dark, congested, or too much like the places near the flood zone.

As these episodes repeated, Nathan had come to believe that the disaster had permanently altered who he was. He told himself he used to be a happy person but was now miserable all the time, and the contrast felt to him like proof that something essential had been lost. Around other officers, and even at home with his wife, he felt set apart, as though no one else inhabited the same world he did anymore. Crowded places began to mean more than inconvenience; they confirmed his sense that he did not belong anywhere, that other people moved easily through spaces that for him remained charged with danger. That belief made him scan more sharply for dark rooms, tight passageways, waterfront locations, or the smell of alcohol, as if his mind were constantly checking whether the world was about to close in again.

The memories themselves deepened those conclusions. Because what returned were mostly pictures and bodily sensations rather than a coherent narrative, Nathan took their force as evidence that he was still trapped in the disaster somehow. After an intrusive image, he would be left thinking that he was isolated from ordinary life in a way other people could not understand. The strangeness of having a memory that felt both vividly physical and unreal only increased his conviction that he was no longer the same man and could not find a place among others. In turn, when he was already telling himself that he belonged nowhere, the next image came faster and landed harder, as if his own bleak conclusions opened the door for the flood scene to take over again.

He responded by punishing himself mentally. When he canceled on friends or sat alone in the darkened part of the house, he told himself he deserved to suffer because of what had happened. Those private reprimands did not quiet anything; they kept him fixed on the event, replaying the images and bodily terror with even greater intensity. The more he withdrew from friends and avoided circumstances that reminded him of the storm, the smaller his world became. His avoidance brought temporary relief, but it also left him more sensitive to the next crowded briefing room, the next waterfront assignment, the next trace of alcohol in a restaurant, because he was living as if these cues were intolerable. At work, this had started to show. He took longer routes to avoid congested parts of the ship and hesitated over duties in dim compartments, worrying that others would notice.

By the time he sought help, Nathan was frightened by how complete the change felt. His wife had told him he was disappearing from their life together, always finding reasons not to see friends, always on edge about where he sat and what he might smell. What finally brought him in was not one dramatic episode but the accumulation of them: the sense that each avoided gathering, each visual flash, each thought that he deserved his misery was tightening his isolation. What he fears most is that this is permanent—that he will remain cut off, unhappy, and unable to stand where other people stand without feeling trapped. What he hopes, though he says it cautiously, is that the disaster might someday feel like something that happened to him rather than somewhere he is still living.
